opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core reason is that we've already seen this movie play out in language. Before GPT-style models, NLP was a zoo of specialized systems, one for translation, one for sentiment analysis, one for summarization, and each of them was brittle and expensive to build. Then we found that a single generalist model, trained at scale, could do all of those tasks better than the specialists. My bet is that robotics is going to follow a very similar trajectory.

Right now most robots are still built the old way. You have one robot, one task, one carefully engineered pipeline, and if you change the lighting or move the object a few inches, it falls apart. That doesn't scale. If we want robots in homes, factories, and hospitals, we can't hand-craft a new system for every single job. We need a foundation model for physical intelligence, something that understands how the world works, can follow instructions, and adapts to new situations without being retrained from scratch.

Humanoids are a big part of why I think a general-purpose approach makes sense. Our world is designed around the human form factor: our tools, doorknobs, kitchens, and factories. A humanoid can, in principle, operate in all of those environments, and a general-purpose humanoid also lets you tap into the largest data source on the planet, which is humans doing things. Every video of a person cooking or folding laundry becomes potentially useful training signal.

The hardest part, honestly, is data. Unlike language models, we can't just scrape the internet for robot actions. So with Groot we think about it as a data pyramid. At the base you have internet-scale video and human data, which is huge but doesn't contain motor commands. In the middle you have simulation and synthetic data, where we can generate essentially unlimited experience using GPU-accelerated physics and generative models. That's where NVIDIA has a real advantage. At the top you have real robot data, which is the most precious and the most expensive, collected through teleoperation. The magic is in mixing all three.

The last piece is the cross-embodiment idea. We don't want a model that only works on one specific robot. We want something like a universal brain that can transfer across different bodies, the way a person can learn to drive a new car pretty quickly. If we get that right, every robot company benefits, and the whole field moves faster. That's really the vision: not just building one great robot, but helping build the brain that powers all of them.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a single generalist model succeeded across NLP tasks and predicts robotics will follow a similar trajectory.

r002.rationale: The candidate argues for a general-purpose robotics foundation model, but does not say it is a prerequisite for producing task-specific specialized generalists.

r003.rationale: The candidate criticizes one-robot, one-task pipelines as brittle and unscalable, but does not say specialist robotics models make short-run results easier to demonstrate.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that I think robotics is about to go through the same transition that language went through with GPT. For decades, the field built one model per robot, per task, per lab. You'd spend a year getting a specific arm to do a specific manipulation in a specific environment, and the moment you changed the gripper or the lighting or the object, you started over. That doesn't scale, and it's not how intelligence works.

With Project GR00T, the bet is that the right abstraction is a foundation model for embodiment. Take a model that understands language, perceives the world, and outputs motor actions, and train it across many bodies, many tasks, and many sources of data. The humanoid form factor is a big part of why this is tractable now. The world is built for human bodies: doorknobs, stairs, kitchens, factory lines. If you commit to that form factor, you can pool data across robots that are morphologically similar, and you suddenly have a shared target instead of a thousand disjoint ones.

The other thing that's changed is the data situation. Language models got lucky because the internet is a giant free corpus of text. Robotics has no internet of actions. So the approach has to be a mixture: real teleoperation data, which is high quality but expensive; simulation, where we can generate orders of magnitude more trajectories with domain randomization; and human video, which is enormous and shows how bodies move through the world even though it lacks the action labels. A general model is the only thing that can actually absorb all three. A narrow policy can't benefit from a YouTube video of someone folding laundry. A foundation model can.

And then there's the flywheel argument. Once you have a general model, every deployment becomes a data source, and every improvement to the base model lifts every downstream skill at once. That's the dynamic that made LLMs compound so fast, and I don't see why embodied intelligence should be different. It's harder, the data is harder, the safety constraints are real, but the direction feels right. I'd rather be building the GPT-3 of robotics, even a rough one, than another beautiful single-task demo.

r001.rationale: The response compares robotics’ coming transition to GPT and says the foundation-model approach could let embodied intelligence compound as LLMs did.

r002.rationale: It says a general model can improve downstream skills, but does not identify it as a prerequisite for producing task-specific specialized generalists.

r003.rationale: It contrasts a rough general model with a polished single-task demo, but does not say specialist models make short-run results easier to demonstrate.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that we shouldn’t have to train a new model for every robot and every task. If you teach a robot to pick up a cup, that experience should help it pick up other objects. And ideally, what it learns should also help a robot with a different body.

That’s the motivation behind Project GR00T: build a foundation model that can learn across tasks and embodiments. The body might change—the sensors, the joints, the way you control the hands—but a lot of the underlying understanding of the world is shared.

The hard part is data. With language models, you have the internet. In robotics, we don’t have an equivalent supply of examples of physical interaction. So we need to bring together real robot demonstrations, information from video, and simulation, where we can generate varied experiences and practice at scale.

The bet is that learning these things together gives us better transfer than building a separate system for each task. Then, when you introduce a new robot or a new skill, you’re adapting an existing foundation instead of starting from scratch.

r001.rationale: The response advocates a robotics foundation model, but it does not say that NLP foundation-model success can be replicated in robotics.

r002.rationale: It says new robots and skills can adapt an existing foundation, but does not identify a general-purpose model as a prerequisite for producing task-specific specialized generalists.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that specialist robotics models make short-term results easier to demonstrate.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that we shouldn’t have to build a new model for every robot and every task. If a robot learns to pick up a cup, some of that understanding should transfer to picking up a bottle. And if one robot learns something useful, we want that experience to help other robots, even when their bodies are different.

That’s the motivation behind Project Groot: build a general-purpose foundation model that can learn across tasks and embodiments, then adapt to a particular robot. The model needs to connect perception, language, and action—to take an instruction, understand the scene, and figure out how to move.

The big challenge is data. Robotics doesn’t have an internet-scale collection of actions sitting there waiting for us. So the approach has to include a way to scale experience, combining real-world demonstrations with simulation. If we can get that loop working, each new task becomes an opportunity to improve a shared model, rather than another system we have to engineer from scratch.
